clinicalPearls: A common cause of acute scrotal pain in prepubertal boys, from twisting of an embryological remnant (usually the appendix testis)
Pain is usually more gradual and less severe than in testicular torsion, and systemic upset is uncommon
The classic sign is a tender blue dot at the upper pole of the testis seen through the scrotal skin
The testis itself lies normally with a normal cremasteric reflex, unlike in testicular torsion
It is a key differential of the acute scrotum, where the priority is to exclude testicular torsion
It is self-limiting and managed conservatively once torsion of the testis is excluded
reference.pathophysiology: The testis and epididymis carry small vestigial embryological appendages. Torsion of one of these pedunculated appendages, most often the appendix testis (hydatid of Morgagni), causes ischaemia and infarction of the remnant with local inflammation and pain. Because the testicular blood supply is unaffected, the testis remains viable, and the process settles as the infarcted appendage necroses and resolves. The main clinical importance is distinguishing it from true testicular torsion, which is a surgical emergency.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment, including looking for the blue dot sign
Doppler ultrasound showing normal testicular blood flow when the diagnosis is uncertain
Assessment of the cremasteric reflex and testicular lie
Surgical exploration if testicular torsion cannot be excluded
redFlags: Features suggesting testicular torsion (severe sudden pain, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex)
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting, resolving over days with conservative management and analgesia, with no long-term testicular consequences.
pitfalls: Missing testicular torsion by over-diagnosing appendage torsion
Delaying exploration when torsion cannot be excluded
Relying on the blue dot sign, which is not always present
Attributing pain to infection without considering torsion
management: First exclude true testicular torsion, since distinguishing the two is the key priority in the acute scrotum
Manage conservatively once torsion is excluded, with simple analgesia or NSAIDs, rest and scrotal support, as the condition is self-limiting
Reassure that the infarcted appendage necroses and resolves over days without long-term testicular consequence
Reserve surgical exploration and excision of the appendage for cases where testicular torsion cannot be excluded or where pain is severe or persistent
Give safety-net advice to return urgently if pain worsens or acute features develop
Involve paediatric surgery or urology in assessment of the acute scrotum
